Decision-Making Capacity and Informed Consent

the four abilities · what consent covers · WIPE exceptions · who decidesCan this patient make this decision now?

Practice
  1. 45-year-old man brought in after a bar fight smells of alcohol and slurs his words A 2-cm scalp cut has stopped bleeding; he refuses stitches and asks to sleep it off Vital signs are normal → Defer the repair and reassess when he is sober → A nonbleeding laceration poses no imminent harm, and alcohol may only temporarily affect his ability to consent, so the repair waits and he is reassessed; a surrogate decides only if he lacks capacity
  2. 70-year-old woman hospitalized with pneumonia wants to go home on day 2 She explains the risks of leaving, including death, and says she accepts them She is alert and oriented; her son demands that she stay → Discharge her against medical advice → She communicates a choice and shows understanding, appreciation and reasoning, so she has capacity and may leave against medical advice; family decides only when capacity is lacking
  3. 78-year-old man is intubated after a stroke and cannot communicate He has no advance directive or health care proxy His wife wants a feeding tube; his adult daughter says he would refuse one → Follow his wife's decision → Without an advance directive or proxy, family members typically decide in the order spouse, adult children, parents, siblings, judging what he would want; two-physician consent is for patients with no surrogate
  4. 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia needs a decision about surgery for a hip fracture Years ago she named her close friend as her health care proxy Her three children disagree with the friend's choice → Follow the health care proxy → A health care proxy holds durable power of attorney and overrules all family members; a court-appointed fiduciary is for patients with no relative or proxy
  5. 30-year-old man arrives unconscious after a car crash with a ruptured spleen and falling blood pressure No family can be reached, and he carries no advance directive The surgeon is ready to operate → Operate without consent → When delay to find a surrogate would raise the risk of death or serious harm, emergency care proceeds without formal consent, on the assumption that a reasonable person would agree
  6. 33-year-old woman with schizophrenia is on an involuntary psychiatric hold She declines removal of a benign-appearing skin mole, citing the scar She is calm, explains the risks and benefits, and repeats her choice → Respect her refusal → Patients on an involuntary hold keep the right to refuse treatment that is not life-threatening, and a psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity
Pairs with Adolescent Confidentiality: consent by and for minors. Delirium: a reversible cause of lost capacity.
Transferable rule

Ask whether this patient can make this decision now; without an emergency, a capable refusal stands, and impairment that may wear off means wait and reassess.
